entries.title: From Iceland to Greenland — Norse settlement around 985–986
entries.dateLabel: circa 985 or 986 CE; historical tradition, not an exact sailing date
entries.dateMeaning: The date window is the evidence's chronological resolution, not the duration of a single journey.
entries.summary: Households from Iceland established Norse farming settlements in southwestern Greenland around 985–986.
entries.detail: Wallace traces Erik's Icelandic household and followers to Greenland; the Danish National Museum dates the Eastern and Western settlements to approximately 985. These sources support a migration connection at year-scale precision.
entries.uncertainty: No exact day, named embarkation beach or itinerary is known from this evidence. Both the Eastern and Western settlements were on Greenland's west side; this endpoint represents the Eastern Settlement.

entries.title: From Greenland to Newfoundland — the Norse connection
entries.dateLabel: Early eleventh-century context; short-lived archaeological samples at L'Anse aux Meadows broadly 990–1050, with cutting activity independently fixed to 1021
entries.dateMeaning: The date window is the evidence's chronological resolution, not the duration of a single journey.
entries.summary: Norse seafarers connected Greenland's settlements with L'Anse aux Meadows on Newfoundland's northern peninsula.
entries.detail: The archaeological site and the 1021 wood date establish activity in Newfoundland. Kuitems and colleagues' regional map locates the Greenland settlements from which the Norse ventured west; later sagas provide differing voyage narratives.
entries.uncertainty: The line is a broad source-region connection. It does not date arrival to 1021, identify the crew as Leif's, or confirm a sequence of Labrador/Baffin landfalls. The 990–1050 window brackets context, not a sixty-year voyage.

entries.title: Igaliku/Garðar — imported North American and European wood
entries.dateLabel: Igaliku wood contexts: phase 1, 1100–1300 CE; phase 2, 1300–1400 CE
entries.dateMeaning: The date window is the evidence's chronological resolution, not the duration of a single journey.
entries.summary: Small amounts of imported wood reached the bishop's farm at Igaliku alongside local wood and driftwood.
entries.detail: Microscopic identification found jack pine and hemlock, taxa assigned to North American sources, with European beech and oak. The author separates these rare imports from the much larger local and driftwood supply.
entries.uncertainty: A particular American forest, landing, ship, intermediary or annual shipment cannot be identified. The later phase contains potentially mixed deposits. No named transatlantic route is plotted from this point.

entries.title: Arctic walrus ivory reached twelfth-century Kyiv
entries.dateLabel: Mid- and late-twelfth-century contexts, shown conservatively at century resolution
entries.dateMeaning: The date window is the evidence's chronological resolution, not the duration of a single journey.
entries.place: Western Greenland and eastern Canadian Arctic walrus-source region
entries.summary: Walrus remains excavated in Kyiv connect its ivory supply with the western Arctic and Norse Greenland's trade network.
entries.detail: Five analysed specimens belong to a genetic clade restricted to western Greenland and Arctic Canada. Their prepared tusk sockets and isotope evidence support the authors' interpretation of trade through Norse Greenland.
entries.uncertainty: The biological source is a wide region. Norse Greenland transit is an archaeological-historical inference; individual hunters, intermediaries, European ports and the complete route to Kyiv are not identified.

entries.title: Qassiarsuk and the Eastern Settlement — Norse farms and later abandonment
entries.dateLabel: Circa 985 to the mid-fifteenth century, regional Eastern Settlement chronology
entries.dateMeaning: 985 and 1450 are approximate regional anchors. They do not establish identical foundation or abandonment dates for every farm at Qassiarsuk.
entries.summary: Norse farming around Qassiarsuk belongs to the Eastern Settlement, whose regional occupation continued into the mid-fifteenth century.
entries.detail: The last surviving dated written event, the Hvalsey wedding in 1408, is distinct from settlement abandonment. Later archaeological evidence prevents treating 1408 as the end of habitation.
entries.uncertainty: The 1450 marker is an inferred, approximate regional abandonment anchor. It is neither the proven date of the last departure nor a dated ending for each Qassiarsuk farm.

endEvidence.label: Abandoned around the mid-1400s
endEvidence.note: 1450 is an editorial anchor for a regional mid-fifteenth-century interpretation. Occupation continued after 1408; no precise last-person departure is known.

entries.title: Independence I camps around Jørgen Brønlund Fjord
entries.dateLabel: circa 2400–1800 BCE; museum chronology for the principal Peary Land phase
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Early communities camped around Jørgen Brønlund Fjord and hunted muskoxen, seals and birds.
entries.detail: The museum locates a major concentration of Independence I camps here. Its terrestrial-bone chronology places arrival around 2400 BCE, with the principal Peary Land population declining around 2000–1800 BCE.
entries.uncertainty: The dates describe a regional archaeological phase. Scattered later determinations do not justify continuous occupation of every camp. This does not identify Greenland's first individual landing.

entries.title: Qeqertasussuk — Saqqaq hunting and island life
entries.dateLabel: circa 2400–1400 BCE, the site-study chronology cited by the museum
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Qeqertasussuk preserves tools, wood and animal remains from Saqqaq people living from the rich resources of Disko Bay.
entries.detail: The preserved assemblage records a varied hunting and gathering economy. The museum's bibliography explicitly identifies the site's 2400–1400 BCE study window.
entries.uncertainty: This broad site phase is not continuous residence by a single household, and the modern point is deliberately generalized.

entries.title: Nipisat — repeated Saqqaq visits to an island hunting place
entries.dateMeaning: Three archaeological occupation phases and their calibrated dating ranges.
entries.summary: Nipisat's hearths and animal remains record repeated seasonal visits by Saqqaq hunters over more than a millennium.
entries.detail: Thirty-three radiocarbon determinations underpin three phases. Tools and food remains reveal marine hunting alongside mainland caribou procurement; the primary report describes short visits in spring, summer and early autumn.
entries.uncertainty: The problematic 520 BCE determination is excluded. The encompassing interval is not year-round or uninterrupted residence.

activityWindows.note: Phase 3, 1310–810 calibrated BCE. A problematic 520 BCE measurement is excluded.

entries.title: Qilakitsoq — Inuit clothing and family history around 1475
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Two graves at Qilakitsoq preserve the clothing and personal histories of eight Inuit people.
entries.detail: The museum dates the burials to approximately 1475. Clothing and the relationships among the people provide unusually detailed evidence of late medieval Inuit life in Greenland.
entries.uncertainty: The approximate date concerns these burials; it does not date all houses at Qilakitsoq, identify the cause of death, or imply an end to Inuit life.

entries.title: Nuuk — a colonial mission house built in 1728
entries.dateLabel: 1728, construction date in the protected-building register
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Hans Egede's house at Nuuk dates to 1728, marking a durable colonial mission establishment on this inhabited coast.
entries.detail: The protected-building register identifies the surviving house as B-37. This local anchor distinguishes Nuuk from the earlier 1721 mission on Hope Island.
entries.uncertainty: The house's construction is not the beginning of Indigenous occupation. The 1721 mission is a different locality.

entries.title: Igaliku — Tuperna and Anders Olsen's family renewed farming in 1782
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Tuperna, Anders Olsen and their family established themselves at Igaliku in 1782 after farming at Upernaviarsuk.
entries.detail: NKA's archaeological report connects the brief 1780–81 Upernaviarsuk farm with the family's move to Igaliku. It situates the renewed farming economy within Inuit and colonial family history.
entries.uncertainty: This is a dated family relocation and farming anchor; it does not imply direct continuity between the medieval Norse and eighteenth-century farms.

entries.title: Nuuk — a provision store on the colonial harbour in 1850
entries.dateLabel: 1850, construction date in the protected-building register
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: A provision store built at Nuuk in 1850 anchors the town's harbour-based supply and trade economy.
entries.detail: The building register records B-43 as a Proviantbod, linking the surviving harbour fabric to nineteenth-century provisioning.
entries.uncertainty: The building date alone does not establish a specific cargo, overseas source port or trade volume.

entries.title: A tephra layer sets a latest date for Reykjavík’s older wall
entries.dateLabel: Wall predates the tephra dated about 871 ± 2 CE
entries.dateMeaning: The time bracket dates the volcanic ash constraint. The wall already stood when that ash fell.
entries.summary: An older wall beneath Reykjavík's later town preserves evidence from Iceland's settlement-period landscape.
entries.detail: The City Museum identifies a wall fragment north of the later longhouse as earlier than 871. The settlement tephra helps constrain the age of the wall.
entries.uncertainty: 869–873 dates the ash horizon, while the construction year and any earlier human activity remain unknown.

entries.title: Reykjavík — a tenth-century household at Aðalstræti
entries.dateLabel: 930–1000 CE, museum chronology of the excavated hall
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: A turf-built longhouse at Aðalstræti records household life in tenth-century Reykjavík.
entries.detail: The excavated hall under the Settlement Exhibition dates to approximately 930–1000 and sits beside an earlier wall, showing multiple phases within the locality.
entries.uncertainty: The hall's archaeological dating does not identify its occupants by a saga name or date all nearby activity.

entries.title: Þingvellir — the assembly landscape from 930 to 1798
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Þingvellir hosted Iceland's assembly, bringing people together for law, disputes and political decisions.
entries.detail: The park dates the assembly's establishment to 930 and its meetings here through 1798. Its powers changed under royal rule; many visible booth remains are later than the Commonwealth.
entries.uncertainty: The interval does not mean uninterrupted independence or unchanged institutions. Visible ruins should not all be assigned to 930.

entries.title: Skálholt — a bishop's seat and centre of learning
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Skálholt became an episcopal centre in 1056 and remained a major place of worship, learning and administration.
entries.detail: The heritage agency traces the bishop's seat through Catholic and Lutheran phases until its formal transfer to Reykjavík in 1801.
entries.uncertainty: The date applies to the institution and archaeological place, not to the present modern cathedral or uninterrupted operation of a particular school building.

entries.title: Hafnarfjörður — German merchants and an Icelandic harbour
entries.dateLabel: circa 1490–1602, German trading dominance before the Danish monopoly
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Hafnarfjörður became an important harbour for German merchants trading with Icelanders.
entries.detail: The cultural-landscape report identifies German dominance after 1490 and its end with the Danish monopoly in 1602. The harbour provided a place where Icelandic production and imported goods met.
entries.uncertainty: The period is approximate and does not date every merchant, building or voyage. No precise shipping track is inferred.

entries.title: Reykjavík — a workshop town taking shape in 1762
entries.dateMeaning: The interval describes the supported archaeological phase or institutional activity, not occupation on every day.
entries.summary: Aðalstræti 10 was built for the Innréttingar enterprises in 1762, part of Reykjavík's growth as a place of manufacturing and work.
entries.detail: The City Museum uses the surviving building to interpret the industrial enterprises and the town's subsequent urban life.
entries.uncertainty: This is a dated building within urban development, not the founding date of Reykjavík.

entries.title: Western Settlement — Norse farms and abandonment around 1350
entries.dateLabel: Late tenth / early eleventh century to approximately the middle of the fourteenth century
entries.dateMeaning: 1000 and 1350 are rounded regional display anchors. Farms were established and left at different times; neither endpoint dates a single arrival or the departure of the last inhabitant.
entries.place: Western Settlement, inner fjords of the present Nuuk region
entries.summary: The Western Settlement has both an approximate beginning and an approximate abandonment, around a century before the Eastern Settlement.
entries.detail: Settlement decline should not be equated with a dated disappearance of every individual. The mapped regional endpoint summarizes archaeological and historical interpretation.
entries.uncertainty: The point represents a fjord region, not modern Nuuk town or a single excavated farm. No destination is inferred for departing residents.

endEvidence.label: Abandoned around the mid-1300s
endEvidence.note: 1350 is an editorial anchor for an approximate mid-fourteenth-century regional abandonment, not an exact final-departure date or confidence interval.

entries.title: Iceland’s continuing population
entries.dateLabel: Settlement from around 870 CE; displayed through 1900
entries.dateMeaning: Continuing population; 1900 is the display ceiling, not a departure or abandonment.
entries.summary: Iceland’s population continues while particular overseas Norse colonies end.
entries.detail: The Icelanders label follows a changing population with origins in the settlement period, including arrivals from Norway and the British Isles. Separate local and institutional records retain their own dates.
entries.uncertainty: The rounded point stands for the island, including its inhabited regions; it does not place an early farm in the interior. Continuity does not mean unchanged ancestry, institutions, religion or Viking-age culture.

entries.title: Hvalsey — a wedding recorded on 16 September 1408
entries.dateMeaning: The historical event is dated to a day. It is an attestation of activity at Hvalsey, not the beginning or end of all Eastern Settlement occupation.
entries.summary: A precisely dated written event within a settlement whose final abandonment is less precisely known.
entries.detail: The church is an identifiable locality. A full construction-to-abandonment lifespan is not asserted here because the checked evidence for this record concerns the wedding.
entries.uncertainty: No departure track or final population count is supplied. The exact date belongs to the wedding; it should not lend false day-level precision to settlement decline.

entries.title: Ari’s account of the papar — a later Icelandic tradition
entries.dateLabel: Íslendingabók composed circa 1122–1133; its papar story concerns an undated period before Norse settlement
entries.dateMeaning: 1122–1133 dates the composition of the surviving textual account. It is not a monk-arrival interval, an occupation duration, a date of surviving manuscript material or an eleven-year voyage.
entries.place: Iceland — place described by Ari’s text, not an identified monastery
entries.summary: A recorded tradition about possible Irish Christian predecessors, presented at the date of the text that attests it.
entries.detail: Papar is normally interpreted here as Irish monks or religious exiles. Their possible presence remains distinguishable from Ari’s securely observable statement. Dicuil’s Thule and Brendan traditions are not promoted into verified tracks.
entries.uncertainty: The reference coordinate is only for Iceland as the subject of the narrative. It is not Ari’s writing desk, Papey monastery, a landing point, or a sailing destination. No precise arrival year or route is assigned.

entries.title: Greenlandic Dorset in the Disko Bay region
entries.dateLabel: About 600 BCE–200 CE in the Disko Bay middens
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate horizon defined by stratigraphy and radiocarbon dating at Sermermiut and Qajaa.
entries.summary: Dorset-associated tools and dwelling evidence record another chapter of life around Disko Bay.
entries.detail: Archaeological categories distinguish technologies and assemblages; they do not identify a single political people. The regional interval does not mean every camp was inhabited throughout.
entries.uncertainty: A regional chronology tied to two midden sequences. The National Museum gives a wider early Greenlandic Dorset bracket of about 700 BCE–200 CE.

entries.title: Younger Independence II evidence near Dove Bugt
entries.dateLabel: About 200 BCE to the start of the Common Era
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate age of some of the younger northeastern Independence II finds.
entries.summary: Dove Bugt preserves coastal finds related to the Independence II archaeological tradition.
entries.detail: Lithic research has linked this category with Early Dorset. Coastal resources and camp settings differed from those farther inland.
entries.uncertainty: The oldest dates near 800–600 BCE apply to wider northern and northeastern evidence. Dove Bugt supplies later dates, and some east-coast measurements on marine bones are sensitive to reservoir correction.

entries.title: Thule ancestors reach Greenland
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The ancestors of present-day Greenlanders reached Greenland around 1200.
entries.detail: Greenland’s museum connects this movement to the Thule tradition from Alaska. Boats, sledges and hunting equipment belong to a long Arctic migration, not one documented voyage.
entries.uncertainty: Approximate museum chronology; no exact landing year or traced route is known.

entries.title: A mission and colonial trading venture at Kangeq
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: Hans Egede’s party landed in Greenland on 3 July 1721.
entries.detail: The mission and commercial venture entered an inhabited Inuit landscape. This marks a colonial undertaking, not Greenland’s first settlement.
entries.uncertainty: Approximate island anchor; the marker does not imply Danish control of the whole island.

entries.title: An Inuit gathering route witnessed near Kangeq
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: Egede recorded large groups traveling north in women’s boats in April 1722.
entries.detail: The account connects movement near the colony to an established seasonal gathering and resource landscape. Indigenous networks predated the colonial post.
entries.uncertainty: A contemporary observation of people passing, not an annual population count or an exact boat track.

entries.title: Cryolite extraction begins at Ivittuut
entries.dateMeaning: Opening and part of the documented operating period. Mining continued beyond 1900.
entries.summary: Mining at Ivittuut connected Greenland to industrial demand for cryolite.
entries.detail: Extraction began in 1854 and continued after the end of this map. The site belongs to an industrial and colonial economy as well as a mineral landscape.
entries.uncertainty: 1900 is only the display ceiling; the source dates mining through 1987.

entries.title: Livestock before the Viking settlement period
entries.dateMeaning: Published age model for the appearance of sheep DNA and increased fecal biomarkers in lake sediment.
entries.summary: Sheep DNA and fecal biomarkers indicate human introduction of livestock centuries before the familiar Norse settlement period.
entries.detail: The age model centers near 500 CE. This is environmental evidence of people and livestock in the watershed.
entries.uncertainty: Published 95% dating interval; it does not identify the settlers as Irish monks or establish continuous occupation.

entries.title: Norse settlement across the Faroes
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate early Norse archaeological settlement horizon.
entries.summary: Norse settlement belongs to the ninth-century expansion across the North Atlantic.
entries.detail: The islands became part of a connected maritime world. Early settlement evidence and later political incorporation answer different questions.
entries.uncertainty: The range brackets a regional archaeological sequence. The date of the first Norse landing and settlement extent are less precise.

entries.title: Faroes within the Norwegian kingdom
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The conventional political chronology places the Faroes under the Norwegian crown in 1035.
entries.detail: The Faroese government’s timeline uses 1035 for formal incorporation and places effective royal rule later, by the late twelfth century.
entries.uncertainty: A retrospective constitutional anchor, not proof of uniform day-to-day control.

entries.title: Faroes remain with Denmark after Kiel
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The Faroes remained under the Danish crown when Norway passed into union with Sweden.
entries.detail: The treaty changed the archipelago’s constitutional relationship while its separate jurisdiction continued.
entries.uncertainty: Treaty relationship; not a claim that the islands had no local political life.

entries.title: The Løgting is abolished
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: Danish authorities abolished the Løgting in 1816.
entries.detail: This changed the island assembly’s institutional role.
entries.uncertainty: The map marks an institutional act, not the disappearance of Faroese identity.

entries.title: A modern written form for Faroese
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: Hammersheimb developed an influential orthography for Faroese in 1846.
entries.detail: Spelling connected a spoken language and oral traditions to a growing written culture.
entries.uncertainty: City reference only; the marker is not the documented desk where the system was written.

entries.title: The Løgting returns as an advisory council
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The Løgting was re-established with an advisory role in 1852.
entries.detail: Restoration did not give it the powers of a modern sovereign parliament.
entries.uncertainty: Institutional date; powers should be read in their nineteenth-century setting.

entries.title: The royal trading monopoly ends
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The end of the monopoly widened opportunities for Faroese commercial trade.
entries.detail: Export-oriented fishing developed in the later nineteenth century.
entries.uncertainty: The date is a legal change, not the beginning of all local exchange or a measured surge on every route.

entries.title: The assembly adopts Christianity
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The adoption of Christianity is conventionally dated to around 1000.
entries.detail: A public religious settlement and household practices did not necessarily change at the same pace.
entries.uncertainty: A historical convention sometimes given as 999/1000; conversion was a process.

entries.title: Icelanders swear allegiance to the Norwegian crown
entries.dateMeaning: Several agreements and acts of submission took place from 1262 to 1264.
entries.summary: Agreements in 1262–1264 changed Iceland’s relationship to royal authority.
entries.detail: The Alþingi continued in altered form.
entries.uncertainty: The range covers acceptance of the agreement, not a single nationwide ceremony.

entries.title: Jónsbók becomes law
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The Jónsbók law code entered Iceland’s legal history in 1281.
entries.detail: Law linked local legal practice with royal authority.
entries.uncertainty: The assembly site is a reference for enactment, not the only place where the law was used.

entries.title: Printing begins under Bishop Jón Arason
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: A press acquired around 1530 helped establish printing in Iceland.
entries.detail: Early production was religious and predominantly Icelandic.
entries.uncertainty: Approximate introduction date; it does not date every surviving edition.

entries.title: Danish trade monopoly regulates Icelandic commerce
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: Royal restrictions governed Icelandic foreign trade from 1602 through 1787.
entries.detail: The legal monopoly shaped access to overseas markets.
entries.uncertainty: Regional institutional anchor, not a single port’s complete shipping history.

entries.title: Laki erupts across the southern landscape
entries.dateMeaning: Periods of fissure eruption and associated effects in 1783–1784.
entries.summary: An eruption beginning in June 1783 continued into February 1784.
entries.detail: The library preserves contemporary accounts of a crisis affecting farms and communities.
entries.uncertainty: Point marks the fissure region, not the footprint of lava, gases or famine.

entries.title: The old Alþingi is abolished
entries.dateMeaning: Abolition of the former assembly in 1800, separate from its last meeting at Þingvellir.
entries.summary: Royal decree abolished the Alþingi in 1800.
entries.detail: The last assembly at Þingvellir took place in 1798. Reykjavík hosted the final meetings in 1799 and 1800 before abolition.
entries.uncertainty: Institutional break; Iceland remained inhabited throughout.

entries.title: Alþingi meets again in Reykjavík
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The restored assembly first met on 1 July 1845.
entries.detail: It began as an advisory parliament.
entries.uncertainty: 1843 authorized restoration; 1845 dates the first meeting.

entries.title: A constitution changes legislative powers
entries.dateMeaning: Dated evidence or institutional change; the qualification below specifies what the date measures.
entries.summary: The 1874 constitution expanded Icelandic legislative responsibilities.
entries.detail: The change came before later home rule and sovereignty.
entries.uncertainty: The marker does not present 1874 as full independence.

entries.title: Parliament moves into a purpose-built stone house
entries.dateMeaning: Inauguration and use through the atlas window. Alþingi continued to meet here beyond 1900.
entries.summary: Alþingi began meeting in its new stone building in 1881.
entries.detail: The building gave the institution a permanent setting in the growing town.
entries.uncertainty: 1900 is the display ceiling; meetings continued later.

entries.title: Early Independence II in northern Greenland
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate age range of the earlier reported Independence II evidence.
entries.place: Peary Land and adjacent northern Greenland
entries.summary: Early Independence II dates occur in Peary Land and northeastern Greenland.
entries.detail: Artefacts and dwellings show regional differences within what lithic research links with early Greenlandic Dorset.
entries.uncertainty: The pin is a northern region anchor. The age range represents early evidence and regional use extended beyond it.

entries.title: Late Dorset in the northwest High Arctic
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate dated Late Dorset horizon in the National Museum’s Greenland overview.
entries.summary: Separate Late Dorset evidence occurs in northwestern Greenland in a later period than the Disko Bay horizon.
entries.detail: Dwelling and artefact evidence supports distinctive settlement practices. Late Dorset and early Thule findings can occur in overlapping centuries across the High Arctic.
entries.uncertainty: The approximate regional range follows one museum synthesis. Earlier Late Dorset dates are proposed in some research and a map pin does not locate a specific excavated dwelling.

entries.title: Inuit communities continue in Greenland
entries.dateMeaning: Broad island-wide continuity from Thule ancestry to the Inuit communities documented in later periods.
entries.summary: The ancestors of present-day Greenlandic Inuit communities reached Greenland around 1200, and Inuit communities continue beyond this timeline.
entries.detail: Broad continuity includes regional moves and changes in practices, economies and colonial contacts. It remains distinct from the later ending of the Norse farming settlements.
entries.uncertainty: The rounded map point stands for Greenland. The interval carries no implication that every district was continuously inhabited or that all Inuit communities share the same local history.

entries.title: A colonial station opens in the inhabited Tasiilaq region
entries.dateMeaning: Establishment of the colonial trade and mission station.
entries.summary: A trade and mission station opened in 1894 in a region already inhabited by Tunumiit.
entries.detail: The Greenland National Museum’s records distinguish existing communities and livelihoods from the later Danish colonial presence.
entries.uncertainty: The entry dates the station rather than early settlement, and its pin represents the town area.

entries.title: Charred barley beneath a Norse-period house site
entries.dateMeaning: Two periods attested by radiocarbon dating of charred barley in older ash deposits.
entries.summary: Two groups of peat ash and charred barley beneath later structures supply direct archaeological evidence of earlier Faroese activity.
entries.detail: Church and colleagues date the earlier combined sample to 351–543 calibrated CE and an upper ash deposit to 601–765 calibrated CE at the published 2-sigma resolution.
entries.uncertainty: Dates describe dated material in distinct layers. They neither identify the settlers nor establish habitation between the dated phases.

activityWindows.note: Weighted age of barley grains in the lower ash deposit, calibrated CE.
Barley grain in the upper ash deposit, calibrated CE.
